doc.title: Ken Peplowski interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Goodman's rehearsals and the Radio City night
summary: Goodman drilled time by cutting the rhythm section; the Radio City fund raiser where he played brilliantly.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: the way he wanted it and I think he liked that. He was a very tough band leader though. We could go through a whole rehearsal and not get past the first eight bars of a tune. Very tough, very demanding, but he got results. And he whipped us into shape and made us sound like a Benny Goodman band. He was no more tough or crazy than Buddy Rich for example.
What was in his instructions that made you sound like a Benny Goodman band?

Well one big thing with him was everybody had to develop their own strong sense of time, of rhythm. One thing that they’ve talked about in books and I’ve experienced this first-hand, he would rehearse the wind players without the rhythm section and sometimes he would start a tune with everybody and then cut the rhythm section out and we’d have to play on our own, swinging, as if the rhythm section was there. And I learned that that’s the way he played. He had such strong time that he could actually bring up a bad rhythm section or a bad band. A very strong sense of time. It’s the kind of thing that you can’t even write it down. You can’t put it in a textbook. You’d have to experience it first hand. But you realize when you’re on your own, if you’re not like self-propelling, if you’re not moving the music forward, then things start dragging or it sounds like a band just playing dots on a piece of paper. And he got us to swing. He got us to play on our own with this internal rhythm. Then when everybody comes together it swings like you can’t believe. And it’s all about listening and as soon as you start a tempo that’s when the time begins. And it was an amazing thing. I’ve never experienced anybody before or since that could rehearse a band like him. And it was a real lesson for me. And also this old frail man would still get up and play these tunes that he’d been playing over and over and over and sound like he’d been playing them for the first time. There were nights when he just blew us off the stage. We did a night at Radio City Music Hall and it was a fund raiser. It was Ella Fitzgerald, Placido Domingo, Sinatra and Benny. So he was, he knew he was in tough company there. And Sinatra was even in the wings watching us. Benny played so good that night, this was a night to remember for me, he played so good we missed all of our entrances. We couldn’t even play, literally. We were just sitting there listening to this guy. I remember “Stealing Apples” that famous Fletcher Henderson thing, chorus after chorus after chorus and we were just dumbfounded. Like something just turned on in him. Louie Bellson was playing drums and even he said, “geez I haven’t heard him play like this since the 40s.”
Wow. It almost sounds like the story I’ve heard about when Charlie Christian was introduced on the bandstand that particular night and he just was inspired to play even beyond himself.
